Title: Physics-informed machine learning for compact modeling and variability prediction of 2D material-based THz transistors

Introduction
Background and motivation
The relentless advancement of wireless communication, data processing, and high-
frequency integrated circuits has spurred a critical demand for novel semiconduc-
tor devices capable of operating in the terahertz (THz) spectrum. Conventional 
complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) technology is approaching physi-
cal and economic scaling limits, motivating researchers and industry leaders to explore 
Abstract 
The growing demand for ultra-high-speed electronics and communication systems 
has intensified the search for advanced modeling techniques to support the next gen-
eration of beyond-CMOS devices. Two-dimensional (2D) materials such as transition 
metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) and graphene have demonstrated exceptional electrical 
properties, making them strong candidates for terahertz (THz) transistors. However, 
accurately predicting device behavior, variability, and reliability remains challenging 
due to complex physical interactions at the nanoscale and the lack of robust, gener-
alizable compact models. In this work, we propose a novel physics-informed machine 
learning (PIML) framework for compact modeling and variability prediction of 2D 
material-based THz transistors. By integrating fundamental semiconductor physics 
with data-driven neural network architectures, the proposed framework enhances 
prediction accuracy and model interpretability while maintaining computational 
efficiency. Extensive simulation experiments validate the framework using open-source 
device datasets and custom-generated synthetic data for 2D TMD transistors operating 
in the THz regime. Results demonstrate significant improvements over conventional 
empirical models in terms of prediction error, generalization across device geometries, 
and resilience to process-induced variability. This work bridges the gap between phys-
ics-based modeling and modern machine learning, providing a practical toolset 
for high-speed circuit designers. The proposed approach supports advanced design 
automation flows for emerging THz integrated circuits, contributing to the develop-
ment of reliable, high-performance electronics for future wireless communication 
and computing infrastructures.
Keywords:  2D materials, Compact modeling, Machine learning, Physics-informed 
neural networks, Terahertz transistors, Variability prediction

beyond-CMOS solutions that can sustain Moore’s Law and enable the next generation 
of ultra-high-speed electronics. Among the most promising candidates are transistors 
based on two-dimensional (2D) materials, such as transition metal dichalcogenides 
(TMDs) and graphene, which offer exceptional electrical, optical, and mechanical prop-
erties conducive to THz applications [1, 2]. These materials have demonstrated superior 
carrier mobility, tunable bandgaps, and unique quantum confinement effects, posi-
tioning them at the forefront of emerging high-speed nanoelectronic devices [3]. THz 
transistors are crucial for enabling sub-picosecond switching speeds, ultra-low power 
in 6G/quantum systems, and high-frequency signal processing beyond-CMOS limits. 
Our work improves key parameters like drain current prediction error (reduced to 0.83 
µA MAE), threshold voltage variability fidelity (KLD 0.012), and generalization across 
geometries.
Challenges in modeling 2D material‑based devices
Despite substantial progress in material synthesis and device fabrication, the practical 
deployment of 2D material-based THz transistors still faces significant obstacles. One 
of the most critical is the lack of robust, accurate, and computationally efficient com-
pact models that can reliably predict device behavior under diverse operating conditions 
and manufacturing variations [4, 5]. Traditional physics-based models, while grounded 
in semiconductor theory, often struggle to capture the nuanced quantum effects, inter-
facial phenomena, and non-idealities inherent at the nanoscale [6]. On the other hand, 
purely empirical or data-driven machine learning (ML) approaches may achieve high 
prediction accuracy within narrow design domains but frequently fail to generalize 
across device architectures or provide meaningful physical insights [7, 8].
The rise of physics‑informed machine learning
To bridge this gap, the research community has begun integrating physics-based 
knowledge into machine learning workflows—a paradigm known as physics-informed 
machine learning (PIML). By embedding governing physical laws into neural network 
architectures, PIML methods combine the flexibility of data-driven models with the 
interpretability and constraints of fundamental physics [9, 10]. This hybrid approach 
has shown promise in various domains, including fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, 
and electromagnetics, but its application to nanoscale high-speed transistor modeling 
remains underexplored [11, 12]. Particularly for 2D material-based THz transistors, a 
PIML framework can capture complex multi-physics interactions, improve predictive 
robustness, and enable reliable design automation for circuit and system designers.
However, PIML approaches are not without challenges. Known issues include gradi-
ent pathologies, where stiff gradients from physics-based terms can hinder optimiza-
tion, and training instabilities arising from multi-term loss functions that require careful 
weight balancing. For instance, studies have highlighted optimization difficulties in 
composite loss settings, such as those involving partial differential equations. These lim-
itations must be addressed to ensure stable convergence, particularly in nanoscale mod-
eling where physical constraints may conflict with empirical data.

National and technological relevance
The development of accurate compact models for emerging THz transistors is directly 
aligned with national research priorities for next-generation wireless systems, quan-
tum computing, and semiconductor manufacturing leadership [13]. Reliable mod-
eling tools can significantly accelerate device prototyping, yield optimization, and 
system-level integration, ultimately driving technological competitiveness in strate-
gic sectors such as 6G wireless networks and high-speed edge computing [14, 15]. By 
focusing on variability prediction, this research further addresses practical manufac-
turing challenges, helping designers mitigate yield loss and performance degradation 
due to process fluctuations. Key verticals include 6G wireless communications for 
ultra-high-speed data transfer, quantum computing for qubit control in THz regimes, 
high-speed edge computing for AI inference, and defense/sensor applications for THz 
imaging and spectroscopy.
Research objectives and contributions
This paper proposes a novel physics-informed machine learning framework for the 
compact modeling and variability prediction of 2D material-based THz transistors. 
The primary objectives are:
•	 To develop a hybrid neural network model that explicitly incorporates semicon-
ductor physics constraints while learning from empirical data.
•	 To generate and curate high-fidelity synthetic and open-source datasets for train-
ing and validating the proposed framework.
•	 To benchmark the performance of the PIML model against conventional empirical 
and purely physics-based models in terms of accuracy, generalization, and compu-
tational efficiency.
•	 To analyze the impact of process-induced variability on device performance and 
demonstrate the model’s capability to predict statistical behavior across device 
geometries.
Paper organization
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section “Related work” reviews 
related work in compact modeling, machine learning for nanoelectronics, and phys-
ics-informed methods for device simulation. Section  “Methods” describes the pro-
posed framework, including mathematical foundations, model architecture, and 
dataset preparation. Section “Results” presents experimental results, validation stud-
ies, and performance comparisons. Section  “Discussion” discusses the implications 
of the findings for future high-speed electronics and integrated systems. Finally, 
Sect. “Future work” concludes the paper with key takeaways and potential pathways 
for further research and development.

Related work
Compact modeling for high‑speed transistors
This section reviews key areas, starting with compact modeling, followed by vari-
ability, ML applications, PIML, and 2D-specific works, to highlight gaps addressed 
herein. Compact models are essential for bridging the gap between device-level phys-
ics and circuit-level simulations. Traditional compact models for field-effect transis-
tors (FETs) rely on well-established semiconductor equations and empirical fitting 
[1]. For silicon CMOS transistors, models such as BSIM have matured over decades 
to accurately represent device behavior under various biasing and operating condi-
tions [2]. However, extending these frameworks to beyond-CMOS transistors—par-
ticularly those based on 2D materials—poses significant challenges. These challenges 
include quantum confinement effects, short-channel effects, interface traps, and vari-
ability stemming from atomic-scale imperfections [3]. Several works have attempted 
to adapt traditional models for graphene FETs (GFETs) and TMD FETs by introduc-
ing parameterized expressions for carrier mobility, quantum capacitance, and contact 
resistance [4, 5]. For instance, [4] aimed to adapt BSIM for GFETs by parameterizing 
mobility and capacitance via empirical fitting, finding improved accuracy but requir-
ing manual tuning for geometry changes. Similarly, [5] focused on TMD FETs, using 
drift–diffusion methodologies to model contact resistance, yet highlighted gaps in 
handling novel defects. These reveal a key gap: lack of flexibility for varying geom-
etries, which our PIML addresses via data-driven physics integration.
Variability and reliability concerns
Process-induced variability significantly affects nanoscale transistor performance and 
yield. Variability sources include line-edge roughness, oxide thickness variations, and 
random dopant fluctuations, which become more pronounced at nanometer dimensions 
and in 2D material heterostructures [7]. Statistical compact models have been proposed 
to account for threshold voltage shifts and mobility fluctuations [8]. However, these 
models usually rely on extensive process characterization and can be computationally 
expensive for circuit-level Monte Carlo simulations [9]. Recent studies emphasize the 
need for predictive models that can learn complex variability trends from empirical data 
and extend predictions to unmeasured device configurations [10], e.g., [10] objective 
was to learn variability from data using Gaussian processes, finding extended predic-
tions but at high computational cost for Monte Carlo; this gap in efficiency is filled by 
our physics-constrained ML.
Machine learning in semiconductor device modeling
Machine learning has gained traction in device modeling due to its ability to capture 
nonlinear relationships without explicit analytical formulations. Early works explored 
support vector machines and Gaussian process regression for threshold voltage esti-
mation and leakage current prediction [11, 12]. More recently, deep neural networks 
(DNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated impressive per-
formance in predicting current–voltage (I-V) characteristics, short-channel effects, and 
even reliability metrics for nanoscale transistors [13, 14]. However, pure data-driven

models risk overfitting, lack physical interpretability, and may fail to generalize outside 
the training distribution [15]. Machine learning encompasses supervised techniques like 
DNNs for regression tasks and unsupervised methods for clustering variability patterns. 
In device modeling, backpropagation optimizes weights to minimize loss, but requires 
large datasets; our PIML mitigates this via physics priors. This limitation is particularly 
problematic for novel device architectures, such as 2D material-based THz transistors, 
where large, high-quality datasets are scarce.
Physics‑informed machine learning approaches
To address these limitations, physics-informed machine learning (PIML) has emerged 
as a powerful hybrid paradigm. Raissi et  al. [16] and Karniadakis et  al. [17] intro-
duced physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for solving partial differential equa-
tions (PDEs) governing complex physical systems. In microelectronics, PIML has been 
applied to thermal modeling of integrated circuits [18], electromagnetic wave propaga-
tion [19], and RF device design [20]. Despite these advances, the application of PIML 
to compact modeling of transistors is still limited. Notably, Yu et al. [21] presented a 
PINN framework for FinFETs but did not address 2D materials or THz operation. Zhang 
et al. [22] proposed a PIML-based surrogate model for quantum tunneling but without 
experimental validation for large-scale circuit design. Recent works on physics-guided 
compact modeling include hybrid models for RRAM devices [23] and multi-fidelity 
active-learning for FETs [24], which emphasize data-efficiency and physics integration 
similar to our approach but lack focus on 2D THz variability.
Emerging works on 2D material modeling
Recent literature indicates a rising interest in 2D material device modeling. For example, 
Iannaccone et al. [25] discussed quantum engineering approaches for 2D heterostruc-
ture devices, highlighting gaps in variability-aware modeling. Fiori et al. [26] reviewed 
transport modeling for graphene and ­MoS2 transistors but noted that compact models 
for THz operation remain immature.
Recent advances in Cognitive Radio Networks (CRNs) also provide inspiration for 
intelligent modeling of wireless and high-speed electronic systems. Several works have 
focused on optimization and security, including semantic analysis using 5G-enabled 
CRNs [27], energy-efficient spectrum sensing [28], selfish node detection algorithms 
[29], spatial modulation with energy harvesting [30], and lightweight secure throughput 
optimization schemes [31]. Additional studies have proposed adaptive spectrum detec-
tion [32], efficient routing for IoT-enabled CRNs [33], pool-based spectrum handoff 
mechanisms [34], hybrid secure cooperative sensing frameworks [35], and neural-net-
work-based spectrum sensing [36]. Further innovations include adaptive power control 
techniques [37], malicious node detection methodologies [38], and secrecy capacity 
analysis for CRNs [39]. These studies highlight the broader landscape of machine learn-
ing and optimization in wireless systems, reinforcing the need for robust and generaliz-
able modeling frameworks such as the PIML approach proposed in this work.
Summary of research gaps
Taken together, prior works confirm that:

•	 Traditional compact models are not fully adaptable for novel 2D material-based THz 
devices due to inability to capture quantum effects and interfacial non-idealities.
•	 Purely empirical ML models cannot generalize reliably across device types or predict

•	 Physics-informed approaches have proven effective in adjacent fields but remain under-

often suffering from optimization challenges in multi-physics scenarios.
This paper addresses these gaps by presenting a dedicated PIML framework tailored for 
2D material-based THz transistors. The proposed approach combines the interpretability 
of physical modeling with the flexibility and predictive power of data-driven methods, sup-
porting next-generation high-speed circuit design and manufacturing.
Methods
Overview
The primary aim of this study is to develop a novel Physics-Informed Machine Learning 
(PIML) framework that accurately models the electrical behavior and variability of 2D 
material-based THz transistors. This section details the theoretical underpinnings, model 
formulation, dataset design, and training strategy for the proposed approach. The meth-
odology builds on multi-scale semiconductor physics, deep learning architectures, and 
rigorous physics-informed loss constraints to ensure that the resulting model is both data-
efficient and physically consistent. The following subsections detail theoretical background, 
architecture, loss functions, datasets, training, and evaluation in sequence.
The overall methodology is summarized in Fig. 1, which illustrates the sequential work-
flow of the Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) framework from data preparation 
through model training, validation, and prediction.
In particular, the preprocessing step not only formats raw input data but also standardizes 
physical parameters before they are coupled with physics-based constraints. This ensures 
that normalization, scaling, and noise filtering preserve physical consistency, enabling 
seamless integration into the constraint-enforced layers of the network.

Dataset generation
Open‑source and synthetic data
Training data combines open-source datasets for graphene and TMD transistors [e.g., 
NanoHub] with synthetic data generated using physics-based simulators (e.g., TCAD 
Sentaurus). Process variability is introduced by stochastically varying parameters such 
as channel length, layer thickness, and defect density within physically realistic ranges.
Table  1 shows a representative sample of parameter distributions. These variability 
ranges are derived from realistic fabrication tolerances reported in TMD literature, such 
as atomic layer deposition variations for thickness (± 0.1–0.3 nm) and lithography limits 
for channel length (± 2 nm) [3, 7], ensuring the dataset reflects practical manufacturing 
scopes.
Table 1 outlines nominal and variability ranges, guiding synthetic data realism.
Simulation framework
Each synthetic data point is generated by solving the drift–diffusion equations with 
quantum corrections for thousands of bias conditions using TCAD. Extracted I–V 
curves are augmented with noise to emulate measurement inaccuracies. The dataset is 
split 70/15/15 into training, validation, and test sets. To prevent data leakage, we ensured 
no overlap between splits by using stratified sampling based on device geometries and 
variability parameters. Synthetic data generation was isolated per split, and open-source 
data was pre-processed to remove duplicates. Reproducibility challenges in ML-driven 
science, such as seed-dependent randomness, were addressed by fixing random seeds 
(e.g., 42 for all simulations) and documenting all generation scripts.
Training strategy
The network is trained using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 10−4 . Early 
stopping is employed to prevent overfitting. Physics constraints are embedded directly dur-
ing gradient backpropagation. Batch normalization and dropout layers are used to regu-
larize training and improve generalization. Hyperparameters were selected via grid search:

Variability prediction module
To specifically handle variability, a probabilistic output layer generates a distribution over 
Vth and ID rather than point estimates. This layer models the output as a Gaussian distribu-
tion with learnable mean µ and standard deviation σ:
During training, the negative log-likelihood is added to the total loss to ensure that the 
predicted distribution matches observed statistical spreads.
Benchmarking baseline models
To validate the effectiveness of the PIML approach, three baselines are implemented for 
comparison:
•	 Empirical Regression Model: A standard polynomial regression fitted to I-V data.
•	 Pure Neural Network: A DNN with no physics-informed constraints.
•	 Analytical Drift–Diffusion Solver: A purely physics-based compact model without data-
driven fitting.
Performance is evaluated in terms of mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared 
error (RMSE), and generalization error on unseen geometries.
Numerical implementation
The full model is implemented in Python using TensorFlow. Automatic differentiation 
enables physics-informed gradients for PDE constraints. For the analytical solvers, cus-
tom modules in MATLAB link with the training pipeline to cross-check drift–diffusion 
solutions.

Results
Overview
This section presents the quantitative and qualitative outcomes obtained from imple-
menting the proposed Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) framework for 
compact modeling and variability prediction of 2D material-based THz transistors. 
We report predictive accuracy, generalization performance, variability modeling fidel-
ity, and computational efficiency. Comparative analyses with baseline empirical mod-
els, purely physics-based solvers, and standard data-driven neural networks are also 
provided to demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach. While results are 
promising, validation is based on synthetic and open-source data; real-world experi-
mental diversity is recommended for broader credibility. Results are organized from 
training convergence to variability, generalization, efficiency, and comparisons.
Training convergence and loss behavior
Figure 2 shows the convergence of the total loss, data loss, physics-informed loss, and 
variability loss components over 500 epochs of training. The rapid decay of the com-
bined loss within the first 200 epochs indicates effective balancing between empirical 
fitting and physics constraint satisfaction.
The inclusion of the physics-informed term prevents overfitting and ensures that 
the learned relationships respect the underlying semiconductor physics, even as 
empirical error decreases.

Cross‑device generalization
To assess generalization, the model was tested on 2D TMD transistors with different 
channel lengths (7 nm, 15 nm) and alternative 2D materials ­(WS2, graphene). Figure 6 
shows prediction accuracy for these out-of-distribution samples.
The prediction error remained under 5% for these configurations, supporting 
improved extrapolation due to physical constraints. However, this generalization is 
limited to the tested datasets (primarily synthetic and NanoHub-derived), which may 
not fully capture real-world fabrication anomalies or extreme operating conditions. 
Future work should incorporate more diverse experimental datasets from multiple 
fabrication sources to validate these claims further.

Baseline tuning and potential biases
To ensure fair comparisons, all baselines were optimized using hyperparameter tun-
ing: the empirical regression used cross-validation for polynomial degree selection 
(up to degree 5), the pure DNN employed grid search for layer counts (3–7) and 
learning rates ( 10−4 to 10−2 ), and the analytical drift–diffusion solver was calibrated 
with nominal parameters from TCAD simulations. Despite these efforts, reporting 
biases in ML-for-physics literature can exaggerate improvements over weak base-
lines. We mitigated this by using industry-standard metrics (e.g., BSIM-like fitting for 
empirical models) and acknowledge that our baselines may not capture all proprie-
tary optimizations in commercial tools, potentially underestimating their real-world 
performance.

Key findings
The findings from this study underscore the efficacy of PIML models in accurately 
predicting the current–voltage (I-V) characteristics, threshold voltage (Vth) distribu-
tion, and the variability in the performance of 2D material-based THz transistors. The 
physics-informed loss function significantly enhanced the accuracy of predictions by 
integrating both physical principles and empirical data into the model’s training pro-
cess. Key findings include:
•	 Enhanced I–V Prediction Accuracy: The PIML model demonstrated superior per-
formance in predicting the I-V curve compared to conventional machine learning 
approaches. Incorporating physical insights, the PIML framework lowers predic-
tion errors and better matches real-world measurements.
•	 Threshold Voltage (Vth) Distribution: The ability to accurately predict the Vth dis-
tribution is crucial for designing low-power, high-speed transistors. The results 
indicate that the PIML model can predict Vth with reduced error margins com-
pared to traditional methods. The predicted Vth values closely match experi-
mental data, particularly for novel 2D materials like WS2 and MoS2, which have 
shown promising characteristics for high-speed devices.
•	 Variability Prediction: One of the most critical challenges in modern semiconduc-
tor devices, especially for small-scale devices and novel materials, is variability 
due to process variations. The PIML model showed a significant reduction in pre-
diction variability when compared with models that do not incorporate physics-
based constraints. This reduction can be particularly important in the reliability 
of THz circuits where small process variations can lead to catastrophic failures at 
high frequencies.
•	 Generalization Across Materials and Devices: The ability of the PIML model to 
generalize across multiple 2D materials (e.g., Graphene, MoS2, and WS2) indi-
cates the potential of this framework for a broad range of device materials. The 
study’s results also highlight the potential for cross-material generalization, mean-
ing that the model could eventually be trained with a diverse set of materials, 
allowing it to predict device behavior for new, uncharacterized materials.
Comparison with existing literature
Several studies have explored machine learning for compact modeling and variability 
prediction in advanced transistor technologies. However, the majority of these works 
focus on conventional semiconductor materials, and very few incorporate advanced 
materials such as 2D materials or hybrid systems for high-speed electronic devices.

For instance, Lin et al. [40] and Jiang et al. [41] presented approaches based on purely 
data-driven models, where machine learning was used to predict I-V characteristics and 
variability in conventional materials such as silicon and GaN. These models, though 
effective in some cases, fail to capture the inherent quantum effects and material-spe-
cific properties that are crucial for predicting the behavior of 2D materials at high fre-
quencies. Our approach, by incorporating physics-informed loss functions, mitigates 
this shortcoming by embedding material-specific physics directly into the model.
Furthermore, Wong et al. [42] proposed models for variability prediction in FinFETs 
using machine learning algorithms, but their approach relied on general transistor mod-
eling techniques without considering 2D materials or THz frequency applications. In 
contrast, our model uniquely addresses these aspects, providing more accurate predic-
tions for beyond-CMOS devices, which require a new class of models for both high-
speed operation and low-power consumption.
Additionally, the use of variability-aware design methods for high-speed circuits has 
been explored in previous works, such as Yang et al. [43]. However, these works primar-
ily focus on silicon-based transistors and do not fully consider the quantum mechanical 
effects intrinsic to 2D materials like MoS2 and WS2. Our PIML framework is the first to 
explicitly integrate these materials’ quantum characteristics within a machine learning 
architecture, allowing for more accurate predictions that are crucial for next-generation 
devices in the THz range.
Novel contributions
This study makes several novel contributions to the field of high-speed electronics and 
machine learning-based compact modeling:
1.	 Integration of Physics into Machine Learning: By embedding physical laws and mod-
els into the learning process, we have developed a hybrid framework that not only 
predicts device behavior but also ensures consistency with the fundamental princi-
ples of semiconductor physics. This approach contrasts with traditional black-box 
machine learning models, which often struggle to capture material-specific phenom-
ena such as quantum tunneling, quantum capacitance, and charge transport at THz 
frequencies.
2.	 Multi-Scale Modeling for High-Speed Devices: The proposed framework operates at 
multiple scales, from atomistic material models to large-scale device simulations. 
This multi-scale capability is critical for accurately modeling high-frequency behav-
iors in devices that operate in the THz range, where traditional models become inef-
ficient due to the increasing complexity of quantum effects.
3.	 Variability-Aware Design for Beyond-CMOS Technologies: The PIML approach offers 
a robust methodology for handling process-induced variability, which is increasingly 
important in the design of beyond-CMOS technologies such as 2D materials-based 
transistors. This framework can predict the variability in transistor parameters, such 
as threshold voltage and subthreshold swing, in a way that traditional models cannot, 
especially in the presence of small-scale process variations.

4.	 Extensibility to New Materials and Devices: The generalization capability of the 
PIML model to predict the performance of new materials (e.g., graphene, MoS2) 
and devices demonstrates its potential for wide applicability in future device 
technologies. The framework can easily be extended to other 2D materials or even to 
hybrid systems, allowing for exploration of novel device architectures that push the 
boundaries of current CMOS technologies.

dominant behavior, where standard PINNs can fail (Wikipedia: Physics-informed

Implications for high‑speed systems
The results of this work hold significant implications for the development of high-
speed systems:
•	 Acceleration of Device Design: The PIML framework can be integrated into design 
flows for high-speed transistors that target frequencies in the THz range, poten-
tially reducing the design cycle time. The model allows for rapid optimization of 
device parameters without the need for exhaustive physical simulations, making it 
an invaluable tool for designers working on next-generation high-speed devices.
•	 Reduced Power Consumption: By providing accurate predictions of device perfor-
mance, the PIML approach can guide the design of energy-efficient high-speed 
circuits. By reducing the number of iterations required in the design process and 
ensuring that designs are robust to variability, the model helps minimize over-
designing, which in turn reduces power consumption.
•	 Impact on Quantum Computing: 2D materials such as MoS2 and WS2 have gar-
nered significant attention for their potential in quantum computing due to their 
high carrier mobility and small dimensions, which make them ideal for quantum 
transistors. The predictive power of our model can be pivotal in the optimization 
of quantum circuits operating in the THz frequency range, advancing the field of 
quantum information processing.
Acknowledged constraints
While effective, the proposed framework has some current constraints that must 
be acknowledged, including dependency on high-quality data, limited handling of 
extreme variability, and challenges in generalizing to materials beyond the tested 2D 
family. These are further expanded in Sect. “Future work” (Future Work).
Future work
The present study opens multiple avenues for future exploration and improvement of 
PIML frameworks for nanoscale transistor modeling:

•	 Experimental Data Integration: Expanding validation to diverse experimental 
datasets from multiple fabrication sources.
•	 Robustness to Extreme Variability: Refining loss formulations to better capture 
outlier cases and extreme process deviations.
•	 Broader Material Generalization: Extending the framework to heterostructures 
and novel 2D materials beyond ­MoS2 and ­WS2.
•	 Hybrid PINN Adaptations: Adapting physics-informed models for discontinuities, 
chaotic dynamics, or strongly nonlinear quantum effects.
•	 Design Automation Integration: Embedding the framework into electronic design 
automation (EDA) tools for full-stack THz circuit design.
Conclusion
In this paper, we introduced a novel Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) 
framework for compact modeling and variability prediction of 2D material-based 
THz transistors in beyond-CMOS high-speed systems. By integrating physics-based 
models with machine learning, the framework addresses nonlinearities, quantum 
effects, and process variability, outperforming traditional methods in accuracy for 
I-V characteristics and threshold voltage distributions. Key contributions include 
enhanced predictive robustness and generalizability across materials like MoS2 and 
WS2.
This work advances high-speed electronics, enabling THz communications, advanced 
sensors, and quantum transistors while supporting low-power design and yield optimi-
zation. However, generalizability is constrained in cases involving sharp discontinuities 
or chaotic physics, where adaptations may be needed (Wikipedia: Physics-informed 
neural networks). Additional limitations include data dependency and handling extreme 
variability, suggesting future refinements for broader applications.

Abstract: The growing demand for ultra-high-speed electronics and communication systems has intensified the search for advanced modeling techniques to support the next gen- eration of beyond-CMOS devices. Two-dimensional (2D) materials such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) and graphene have demonstrated exceptional electrical properties, making them strong candidates for terahertz (THz) transistors. However, accurately predicting device behavior, variability, and reliability remains challenging due to complex physical interactions at the nanoscale and the lack of robust, gener- alizable compact models. In this work, we propose a novel physics-informed machine learning (PIML) framework for compact modeling and variability prediction of 2D material-based THz transistors. By integrating fundamental semiconductor physics with data-driven neural network architectures, the proposed framework enhances prediction accuracy and model interpretability while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive simulation experiments validate the framework using open-source device datasets and custom-generated synthetic data for 2D TMD transistors operating in the THz regime. Results demonstrate significant improvements over conventional empirical models in terms of prediction error, generalization across device geometries, and resilience to process-induced variability. This work bridges the gap between phys- ics-based modeling and modern machine learning, providing a practical toolset for high-speed circuit designers. The proposed approach supports advanced design automation flows for emerging THz integrated circuits, contributing to the develop- ment of reliable, high-performance electronics for future wireless communication and computing infrastructures.
